excerpt: How to write and save a document in a browser when Word is not installed, what happens when the internet drops, and how to send the file to somebody who has no Google account.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to write a document in Google Docs when Word is not installed. You will create it, format it, save it to the cloud, and download a copy for somebody without a Google account. You only need a browser and an account.

Google Docs is a word processor that runs inside the browser. The document lives in your Google account rather than on the machine, and it saves as you type, which is why the light going out mid-sentence no longer costs you the afternoon.
Before you start

items: A browser and a Google account you can sign in to.
About twenty minutes.
No Word, no installation, and no paid plan.

body.text: Open it and write

items: Type docs.google.com in the address bar yourself, rather than following a link.
Click Blank to start a new document.
Click the words Untitled document at the top left and type a real name.
Type your work in the page, and watch the small note at the top saying Saved to Drive.
Use the toolbar for bold, size, and alignment, exactly as in Word.
Press Ctrl and S if you want to be certain, although saving happens already.

body.text: You will see the word Saved appear beside the title within a second or two of typing, sometimes followed by All changes saved in Drive. That note is the difference between this and a document living only on the screen.

body.alt: A browser showing a Google Docs document open with a title.
body.caption: The word Saved at the top is the proof it is stored. A document that shows Saving is still on its way.

body.text: It looks like a browser document is less serious than a Word file. It is the same text, it exports to Word and PDF, and schools now accept it as a shared link.
Format it like a letter
Everything from the letter lesson applies here: one font, real margins, and space between paragraphs.

items: Set the font to Arial or Times New Roman at size 11 or 12.
Open File, then Page setup, and set the margins to 2.5 cm.
Use Enter between paragraphs rather than pressing space repeatedly.
Add page numbers from Insert, then Page numbers.
Use headings from the style box, which builds a document outline for long work.
Change the language to English (Nigeria) so the spell check behaves.

body.text: None of this is locked in. A Google Doc can be edited by you and by anyone you invite, for as long as the account exists.

body.alt: A learner typing a document in a browser window.
body.caption: One font and real margins. A browser word processor reads exactly like the one installed on the machine.

body.text: Send it to somebody without a Google account
A link is convenient, and a file is safer when the reader may not have internet or an account. Download a copy for official submissions.

items: Open File, then Download, then PDF for a document you are submitting.
Choose Microsoft Word for a file the office must edit.
Rename the download with your name and the purpose.
Attach the file to an email rather than sending only a link.
Keep the Google Doc as your working copy, and export again if you change it.
Do not send an editable link to a form that must not change after submitting.

body.text: Do not worry about the internet dropping. Offline mode can be switched on in the settings, and the document syncs when the connection returns.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is recoverable, and the first two are the ones that worry people most.

items: The page will not load: check the connection, then open docs.google.com again rather than reloading a stale tab.
Your work disappeared: open Drive and look in Recent, then in the Trash for thirty days.
The document is read-only: you are signed out, or the owner gave you view-only access.
The formatting changed after export: fonts that are not installed on the machine are substituted. Use Arial.
The recipient cannot open the link: they need permission. Set it to anyone with the link can view.
Two people edited at once and the text looks odd: check Version history under File to see who changed what.

body.text: Practice
One real document, exported and emailed, and the tool is yours.

items: Create a document and give it a real name.
Set the font, margins, and language.
Add page numbers and one heading.
Download it as a PDF and open the PDF to check it.
Email the PDF to yourself and open it on a phone.

body.text: You can now write anywhere there is a browser, and send the result to anybody. In the next lesson you will share a file without making it public by accident.

excerpt: The difference between a link and a public file, how to give one person access, and how to take that access away again.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to share a file with one person without publishing it to the world. You will set the right permission, copy a link that works for them, and remove access when it is no longer needed. The default setting is not always the safe one.
A shared file has two parts: who can open it, and what they can do once inside. Getting the first right is privacy, and getting the second right is safety. Both live in the same small dialog.
Before you start

items: A file in Google Drive, OneDrive, or a similar service.
The email address of the person who needs it.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Three levels of access

items: Restricted: only the people you name can open it. This is the safest and the correct default.
Anyone with the link: anybody who has the address can open it, including people you did not send it to.
Public on the web: discoverable by search engines, which is almost never what you want for a document.
Viewer: they can read it and cannot change it.
Commenter: they can suggest and comment, which is right for a draft.
Editor: they can change the file, so give this only to people you trust with it.

body.text: You will see a small panel open with a box for names and a drop-down showing the current permission. Read the drop-down before you press Send, because it is remembered for the next file too.

body.alt: A sharing dialog showing permission options for a file.
body.caption: Read the drop-down, not only the name box. The permission decides whether a stranger with the link can open it.

body.text: It looks like anyone with the link is easier because there is nothing to type. It is easier, and it is how a private document ends up forwarded to somebody you have never met.
Share with one person properly
The named method is safer and just as quick once you have done it twice.

items: Right-click the file and choose Share.
Set the general access to Restricted.
Type the person's email address in the box.
Choose Viewer, Commenter, or Editor.
Add a short message that says what the file is.
Press Send, and confirm the person appears in the list below.

body.text: None of this needs a paid account. Named sharing works on the free tier for any file you own.

body.alt: A person sharing a document from a laptop.
body.caption: Name the person, choose the permission, send. Three decisions, and one of them matters more than the others.

body.text: Take access away
Sharing is not permanent, and removing access is part of using it well.

items: Open the same Share panel and find the list of people.
Click the drop-down beside a name and choose Remove.
For a link, change the general access back to Restricted.
Check the file again from a private window, to see what a stranger sees.
Remove access when a project ends, especially for contractors.
If a file was shared by mistake, remove the access before you send an apology.

body.text: Do not worry about offending anybody by removing access. It is normal housekeeping, and the person rarely notices or minds.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is fixable, and the first one is the most urgent.

items: You shared a private file with the link setting: set it to Restricted now. Copies already downloaded cannot be recalled.
The person cannot open it: they must sign in with the exact address you used.
You cannot find the Share button: right-click the file, or use the icon at the top right of an open document.
Somebody changed your document: use Version history to see what changed and restore an earlier version.
You were asked for edit access to a form: give view only, unless they truly must change it.
A link appears in a public place: the file is public. Change the access and tell whoever needs to know.

body.text: Practice
One file shared, one permission removed, and the habit forms.

items: Share a practice file with your own second address as Viewer.
Open it from that second address and try to edit it.
Change the permission to Editor and try again.
Set the general access to Restricted and test the link in a private window.
Remove the second address from the list.

body.text: You can now give somebody exactly the access they need and take it back. In the next lesson you will comment on a document instead of rewriting somebody's sentence.

excerpt: How to leave a comment, suggest an edit instead of making it, and resolve a discussion so the document stays readable.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to comment on a document and suggest edits without changing the author's words. You will leave a comment, make a suggestion, and resolve a discussion when it is finished. This is how offices review work without argument.

A comment is a note in the margin that starts a conversation. A suggestion is a proposed change the author can accept or reject. Neither one edits the document, which is why they are safer than typing over somebody's work.
Before you start

items: A Google Doc or a Word file you are allowed to edit.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: Leave a comment

items: Select the words the comment is about.
Click the small comment icon, or press Ctrl, Alt and M in Google Docs.
Type your note, addressed to a person by name if there are several readers.
Press Comment, and a box appears in the margin.
Reply inside the same box to keep the conversation together.
Click Resolve when the matter is finished, which hides the box without deleting the record.

body.text: You will see the selected text turn yellow and a small box appear at the side with your name and the time. The author receives a notification, which is why comments are better than a message on WhatsApp that nobody can find later.

body.alt: A document with a comment box open beside highlighted text.
body.caption: Select, comment, and resolve. A comment points at the exact words, which is what makes it useful.

body.text: It looks like a comment is the same as an edit. It is not: the words stay untouched until the author accepts a change, which keeps the author in control of their document.
Suggest instead of changing
When you think a sentence should change, suggest it. The author sees both versions and decides.

items: Open the editing mode drop-down at the top right and choose Suggesting.
Type the change you would make, in the place it belongs.
Your text appears in a different colour, with a box asking the author to accept or reject.
Add a one-line comment if the reason is not obvious.
Switch back to Editing when you are working on your own document.
In Word, use Track Changes from the Review tab for the same result.

body.text: None of this damages the document. A rejected suggestion disappears cleanly, and an accepted one becomes ordinary text.

body.alt: A document in suggesting mode showing a proposed change.
body.caption: Suggesting keeps both versions visible. The author chooses, which is the point of a review.

body.text: Keep the margin readable
Twenty open comments make a document hard to read. Tidy them as you go.

items: Resolve a comment once the change is made, rather than leaving it open.
Keep one thread per topic, instead of three comments on the same sentence.
Address the person by name when you want an answer from them.
Write what you want changed, not only that you dislike it.
Check the resolved list before deleting anything permanently.
For a long review, comment on the first page and send the writer a message about the pattern.

body.text: Do not worry about being direct in a comment. Clear notes save an hour of misunderstanding, and a polite sentence costs nothing.
If it goes wrong
These six cases cover most review problems, and each one is a short fix.

items: You cannot comment: you have view-only access. Ask for Commenter rights.
The comment icon is missing: the document is a PDF, which needs a different tool.
Your suggestion was rejected: that is the author's decision. Ask for a reason if you need one.
A comment disappeared: it was resolved rather than deleted. Open the comment history to see it.
The document is full of tracked changes: use Accept all only if you are the author.
Two people edited the same line: use Version history to see both versions, and keep one.

body.text: Practice
One review done properly, and you will prefer it to rewriting.

items: Open a practice document and select a sentence.
Leave a comment that asks a specific question.
Reply to your own comment, then resolve it.
Switch to Suggesting and propose one change.
Accept or reject the suggestion, and check the text.

body.text: You can now review somebody's work without taking it over. In the next lesson you will sort a spreadsheet column without scrambling the rows beside it.

excerpt: How to sort a list without separating names from their amounts, why the whole table must be selected, and how to get back to the original order.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to sort a spreadsheet without scrambling it. You will sort a whole table by one column, keep each row together, and restore the original order if you need it. Sorting a column alone is the mistake that ruins a list of customer payments.

A spreadsheet stores rows, and each row is one record: a name with its amount, a date with its item. Sorting reorders whole rows. Sorting a single column reorders only that column, and the names no longer match their amounts.
Before you start

items: A spreadsheet with a list of at least ten rows.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: Sort the table, not the column

items: Click one cell inside your data, not a whole column.
Press Ctrl and A once to select the current block of data.
Open Data, then Sort range, and tick that the range has a header row.
Choose the column to sort by, and whether it is A to Z or Z to A.
Press Sort, then read the first three rows to confirm names still match amounts.
If it looks wrong, press Ctrl and Z at once, which restores the order completely.

body.text: You will see the header row stay at the top while the data beneath it reorders. That is the sign you sorted the table rather than a column, and it is worth checking every time.

body.alt: A spreadsheet with the sort menu open and a header row visible.
body.caption: Tick the header box, and sort the whole range. The header staying put is the sign that rows stayed together.

body.text: It looks like clicking the column letter and pressing sort is faster. It is faster, and it separates every name from its figure, which is the most expensive spreadsheet mistake there is.
Keep a way back
A sorted list has lost its original order unless you plan for it. Two habits make sorting reversible.

items: Add a numbered column first, such as 1, 2, 3, so you can sort back to the starting order.
Or save a copy of the sheet before sorting, named with the date.
Use Ctrl and Z immediately if a sort went wrong, before any other action.
Sort by date when you want the newest at the top, which is usually more useful than alphabetical order.
Do not merge cells inside a table, because sorting refuses to run on merged rows.
Freeze the header row from View, then Freeze, so it stays visible while you scroll.

body.text: None of this takes more than a minute, and the numbered column has saved more bookkeeping than any filter.

body.alt: A sorted spreadsheet list with matching names and amounts.
body.caption: Names still beside their amounts. That is the check, and it takes three seconds.

body.text: Filter instead of sorting
Sometimes you do not want to reorder the list. You want to see part of it, which is what a filter does.

items: Select the data and choose Data, then Create a filter.
Small arrows appear in the header row.
Click an arrow and choose the values you want to see.
The other rows are hidden, not deleted, and they return when you clear the filter.
Use a filter to answer questions like which payments are unpaid.
Clear the filter before you print or share, or the reader sees a partial list.

body.text: Do not worry about hiding data by accident. A filter is a view, and the rows are still there underneath it.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a repair, and the first is the one to act on fastest.

items: The names no longer match the amounts: undo at once with Ctrl and Z. If you already saved, restore the copy.
The header row sorted into the data: undo, then sort with the header box ticked.
Sorting refuses to run: there are merged cells in the range. Unmerge them first.
Some rows did not move: they were outside the selected range. Select the whole block again.
The filter hides rows you need: clear the filter from Data, then Remove filter.
The list has lost its original order and no numbers were added: sort by a date column, or restore your saved copy.

body.text: Practice
One table, sorted three ways, with the original order kept.

items: Make a table with Name, Amount, and Date, and ten rows.
Add a numbered column from 1 to 10.
Sort by Amount, largest first, and check two names still match their figures.
Sort back to the original order using the numbered column.
Apply a filter and clear it again.

body.text: You can now put a list in order without breaking it. In the next lesson you will print a spreadsheet that fits on one page instead of six.

excerpt: How to fit a wide spreadsheet onto one page, repeat the header row on every page, and check the print preview before you spend money at a business centre.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to print a spreadsheet that fits the paper. You will set the page to landscape, fit the columns to one page, and repeat the header row on every sheet. Without these three settings, a wide table prints across six pages and is unreadable.
A spreadsheet has no page edges on screen. The program decides where the paper ends, and by default it decides badly for wide tables. The print settings are how you take that decision back.
Before you start

items: A spreadsheet with several columns.
About fifteen minutes, and no printer needed for the setup.

body.text: Three settings that fix most tables

items: Open Page Layout, then Orientation, and choose Landscape for a wide table.
Choose Width: 1 page so that every column fits across the paper.
Open Print Titles and set the header row to repeat on every page.
Set the margins to Narrow, which buys two or three characters of width.
Choose Fit to 1 page wide rather than Fit to 1 page, which shrinks the text too far.
Press Ctrl and P and read the preview before you print anything.

body.text: You will see faint dotted lines appear on the sheet showing where the pages will break, and the preview will show the same table on one page instead of three.

body.alt: A spreadsheet print preview showing a fitted table on one page.
body.caption: Read the preview before you print. The page count is the cheapest information in the whole process.

body.text: It looks like fitting to one page is always right. A long list of two hundred customers needs several pages, and shrinking it to one makes it unreadable. Fit the width, not the height.
Make the printed page readable
A printed sheet is read on paper, in a hand, often by somebody older than you. A few choices help.

items: Keep the font at 10 or 11 point after fitting, and check the preview at full size.
Repeat the header row, so page two is still understandable.
Add gridlines in the print options if the table is hard to follow.
Print in black and white unless the colours carry meaning, since many offices print in grey.
Use a plain font, and avoid coloured cell backgrounds that photocopy badly.
Add a title row with the sheet name and the date, so a loose page can be identified.

body.text: None of this changes the data. Print settings live with the file, so the next person who opens it gets the same layout.

body.alt: A printed spreadsheet fitting neatly on one sheet of paper.
body.caption: Landscape, one page wide, repeated header. Three clicks, and the sheet reads like a document.

body.text: At the business centre
A wide sheet printed at a shop costs money per page. Ten minutes of preparation removes most of the waste.

items: Save and take the file as a PDF, so the layout cannot change on their computer.
Or use Export as PDF in Google Sheets, which keeps the fit settings.
Print one page first and check it before the rest.
Ask for the price per page before the job starts.
Ask for double sided if the list runs to several pages.
Check the first page before they print the others.

body.text: Do not worry about asking for a test page. A shop that refuses one is telling you something useful about the rest of the service.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is a settings change, and none of them touches your figures.

items: One column prints on its own page: set Width to 1 page in the page setup.
The text is too small after fitting: reduce the number of columns, or use landscape and narrow margins.
The header is missing on page two: it was not set as a print title.
The gridlines are invisible: turn on Print gridlines in the print settings.
The last column is cut off: increase the left margin, or set the print area to exclude an empty column.
The shop's computer prints differently: send a PDF rather than the spreadsheet file.

body.text: Practice
Set it up once, and every future print of that sheet works.

items: Open a wide table and read the page count in the preview.
Set landscape, then width to one page, and read the page count again.
Set the header row to repeat.
Reduce the margins and check the font is still readable.
Save as PDF and open the PDF to confirm the layout.

body.text: You can now print a table that somebody can actually read. In the next lesson you will build a simple invoice that a customer can pay from.
